topics.label: Understand
topics.heading: What is financial aid?
topics.summary: Financial aid helps students and families pay for university.
points: Minerva looks at your family's financial situation to understand how much help you need. This is called financial need.
Students and families are expected to contribute. Aid may help with some of the costs.
topics.note: Aid depends on available funding, so an offer is not guaranteed. Minerva may consider financial need in admissions.

topics.label: How it works
topics.heading: How does Minerva decide?
points: The student applies for aid. The family helps provide financial information.
Minerva reviews the forms and supporting records. Tax returns are one part of the picture.
Minerva considers the family's finances, what the family can contribute, and the funding available.
If the student qualifies, Minerva may offer a mix of support.

topics.label: Your role
topics.heading: What can parents do?
points: Help gather employment and income records, tax returns or local equivalents, bank statements, and any other records Minerva requests.
Complete the official application, check what Minerva requests, and submit it through the official services. The student keeps control of their private answers.
topics.note: Keep real financial details and documents out of Parent Hub.

topics.label: Forms
topics.heading: Which forms does the student use?
points: Apply to study at Minerva. This is separate from applying for financial aid.
Complete this form about family finances on College Board to apply for aid. Minerva requires it for international applicants too.
After submitting the CSS Profile, use Minerva's Financial Aid Center to answer additional questions and submit the requested records.
topics.note: The student submits through College Board and Minerva. Parent Hub is for planning.

topics.label: Aid offer
topics.heading: What might an aid offer include?
points: Support that generally does not have to be paid back. Minerva calls this type of need-based support a scholarship.
Money the student borrows and must repay under the loan terms.
An opportunity to earn money through work.
topics.note: The amount Minerva expects the family to contribute toward educational costs. It is a cost for the family to plan for. The mix of aid varies with the family's circumstances and available funding.

steps: If your student needs aid to attend, they must apply during their admissions cycle, before receiving an admissions decision.
Use College Board for CSS Profile and Minerva for its Financial Aid Questionnaire.
Confirm the intake, round, year, and cutoff with Minerva before planning.
Find household income and bank records
Minerva lists income records such as tax returns or local equivalents, and 12 months of parent or guardian bank statements. Have your student check the exact requests in their Financial Aid Center.
Keep the original and ask which translation format Minerva accepts.
Keep reported amounts separate from conversions and double-check who each amount belongs to.
Check the places Minerva tells you to submit. Ask Financial Aid who can submit and view parent records.
terms: income
Gross and net income
Gross pay is pay before deductions. Net pay is what remains after deductions.
2,000 gross minus 350 in deductions leaves 1,650 net.
A form may ask for income before deductions rather than the bank deposit.
gross salary net salary take home pay remuneration
deductions
Taxes and mandatory deductions
Income tax is a tax on earnings. Payroll deductions can also include required insurance or social contributions.
A payslip lists 200 in withheld tax and 100 in social insurance.
Record each line separately and distinguish withholding from a final tax bill.
tax withholding paye mandatory payroll deduction social insurance
pension
Pension contributions and pension income
A contribution pays into a retirement plan. Pension income is a payment received from a plan.
A worker contributes 120. A retired person receives a pension payment of 900.
A contribution and a payment received describe different flows of money.
retirement cpp qpp pension
accounts
Savings and checking accounts
Checking accounts commonly support everyday payments. Savings accounts commonly hold money set aside.
A salary arrives in an everyday account. Emergency funds are kept in savings.
Check the account holder, reporting period, currency, and balance listed on the statement.
bank current account deposit balance savings checking
debt
Loans, debt, and installment payments
A loan is borrowed money. Debt is what is owed. Installments are scheduled payments.
A loan has a 3,000 balance and a 150 monthly payment.
An outstanding balance and a monthly expense answer different questions.
borrow liability debt repayment monthly installment
assets
Assets and liabilities
An asset is something of value you own. A liability is a financial obligation you owe.
A property may be an asset and its mortgage a liability.
Keep ownership value and outstanding debt separate unless a form tells you how to combine them.
assets liabilities equity property mortgage investments
benefits
Government benefits and allowances
Benefits can be payments from a public program. An allowance can mean a payment or a tax-related amount, depending on the label.
A child benefit paid monthly differs from a tax-free allowance.
Keep the original label and confirm how the form treats the specific program.
government benefit allowance child subsidy public program
aid-types
Scholarships, grants, and student loans
Scholarships and grants generally do not require repayment if their conditions are met. Loans generally must be repaid.
An award lists a 1,000 grant and a separate 1,000 loan.
Check which part of an offer is funding you would repay.
scholarship grant bursary student loan award
ownership
Parent income and student income
Separate income by the person who earned or received it.
A student's summer wages and a parent's salary belong in different records.
Check which person and time period the question asks about before combining anything.
parent student earnings wages income ownership
